Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks
item.description:
Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 11:17
Mansour Abbas says the prime minister's speech vilifying Palestinian parties put him at risk
Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks on during a speech on the opening day of the new Israeli parliament in Jerusalem on 10 November 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off

The leader of the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said on Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held private talks with him through a close associate, despite publicly branding Palestinian parties "terror supporters who hate Israel".

"He was interested in our position on the law barring an indicted lawmaker from serving as prime minister, and whether we really intended to enter a coalition and replace Netanyahu's government," Abbas told Kan public radio.

"When it serves his interests, Arab citizens suddenly become legitimate, he becomes 'Abu Yair', and Mansour Abbas becomes a worthy partner in his eyes."

The Palestinian-led United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List won a record 19 seats combined, following a surge in turnout among Palestinian voters in Israel, giving them the balance of power.

In a speech to parliament on Tuesday evening, Netanyahu said the United Arab List and the Joint List were seeking to end Israel’s existence, adding that the two parties disagreed only on "what kind of state will arise on its ruins".

"What is the true goal of these factions?" Netanyahu said. "Is it only to improve the socioeconomic conditions of Arab citizens in Israel? We have no problem with that. But that is not their real goal."

Addressing those considering forming a government with Palestinian parties, Netanyahu added: "Don't you understand what they really want to achieve? What their national aspiration is?"

Abbas said Netanyahu’s speech had put him and his family in danger. Asked whether he had received threats, Abbas replied: "There are threats from several directions."

Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
Read More »

"As a party, we have made peace one of our core principles," Abbas said. "To accuse us of supporting terrorism is simply false and always has been. We are law-abiding citizens."

In an interview with Channel 12, Abbas also rejected Netanyahu’s claims about his party’s objectives.

"We do not want to establish an Islamist state or an Arab state," he said. "We have defined ourselves as citizens within the State of Israel. We support peace and ending the conflict through a two-state solution."

Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader tasked by the president with forming a government, described Netanyahu’s speech as "delusional, divisive, hateful and disgraceful".

His Yashar party said it had scheduled coalition talks with Netanyahu’s Likud party, but cancelled the meeting following the prime minister’s address.

"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," Eisenkot wrote in a post on X. 

"I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

item.title: HSBC 'sharia-compliant' fund to exclude arms companies after Israeli-linked revenue exposed
item.description:
HSBC 'sharia-compliant' fund to exclude arms companies after Israeli-linked revenue exposed

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 10:11
Move comes after MEE revealed HSBC’s Islamic Global Equity Index Fund purchased shares in world’s second-largest arms company
A branch of HSBC bank on a street in central London on 27 October 2026 (AFP)
Off

The UK’s largest “sharia-compliant” fund is divesting from companies which take more than 5 percent of their revenue from weaponry, after Middle East Eye revealed last month that it purchased more than $100m worth of shares in companies linked to the Israeli military in the first half of this year.

The new change means the British banking giant HSBC’s Islamic Global Equity Index Fund is expected to divest from major companies including RTX, Rolls-Royce, Honeywell International, BAE Systems and Palantir.

The HSBC fund began tracking the S&P Global 1200 Shariah Select Index, a benchmark of companies screened for compliance with Islamic finance principles, in March. The fund is passively managed, which means it mirrors the index's investments.

In early November, the index updated its methodology and is set to implement the changes on 23 November. It will now exclude defence and weapons companies, military contractors and related sectors from the index.

According to the new criteria, the index will exclude companies with a more than 5 percent exposure to military contracting, nuclear weapons, depleted uranium, incendiary weapons, biological weapons and small arms, among other types of weaponry.

According to most screening guidelines, businesses can be deemed “sharia-compliant” if less than 5 percent of their income derives from sources categorised as impermissible.

The index did not previously exclude companies with exposure to most types of weaponry.

The HSBC fund is overseen by a board of Islamic scholars.

MEE reported last month that the fund purchased $35.7m worth of shares in RTX, the world’s second-largest arms company, in the first half of 2026.

Raytheon, an RTX subsidiary, has been described by Campaign Against the Arms Trade (CAAT) as a “significant supplier of missiles and other goods and services to the Israeli military” and as “implicated in Israel’s war on Gaza”. 

As an arms company, RTX is now expected to be excluded from the index.

Multiple major companies to be excluded

MEE also reported that the HSBC fund purchased $18.9m worth of shares in Honeywell International, a US conglomerate which designs sensors and guidance devices used in weaponry. 

Honeywell manufactured an inertial measurement unit - used to aid precision targeting - which was found in a missile that attacked a school in Gaza in June 2024 and killed at least 40 Palestinians, including 14 children and nine women. 

Nearly 20 percent of Honeywell's revenue comes from military weapons, meaning it is now expected to be excluded from the index.

HSBC to review Islamic fund’s $38m investment in Palantir
Read More »

MEE further reported that the HSBC fund purchased $17.6m worth of shares in Rolls-Royce, which produces engines for Merkava tanks, used extensively by Israel in Gaza, as well as Israeli ships through its German subsidiary MTU. 

Since over 12 percent of Rolls-Royce's revenue comes from military weapons, it is set to be excluded from the index.

The fund also holds 386,784 shares with a current market value of around $9.4m in BAE Systems - Britain’s largest arms company, which manufactures components for F-35 fighter jets. F-35s have been used by the Israeli military in Gaza.

BAE Systems is also set to be excluded from the index.

Hyphen reported last month that HSBC’s fund purchased $38.3m worth of shares in Palantir, the US data surveillance firm with links to Israeli abuses in occupied Palestine.

Palantir does not manufacture weapons, but in January 2024 it announced a partnership with the Israeli Ministry of Defence to deploy its technology in support of “war-related missions” that use drone-fired missiles to target civilians in Gaza, including journalists and aid workers.

In late October, it emerged that HSBC would review the fund's investment in Palantir. The bank said it "take[s] any concerns from our clients seriously and will review this matter carefully, in partnership with independent expert advisers, to assess whether the approach still meets investors’ expectations".

Since military contracting will now be excluded from the index, it is likely that Palantir will be removed.

item.title: She saw her husband and daughter off to Egypt. An Israeli sniper killed her on the way home
item.description:
She saw her husband and daughter off to Egypt. An Israeli sniper killed her on the way home

Submitted by Maha Hussaini on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 11:07
Hours after bidding farewell to her family members leaving Gaza for medical treatment, a Palestinian mother is shot dead
Relatives mourn Noura Sheikh al-Eid, 54, who was killed by Israeli forces in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, on 5 November 2026 (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE)
Off

Noura Sheikh al-Eid bid farewell to her husband and daughter as they left Gaza for medical treatment in Egypt.

It was meant to be a temporary goodbye.

But as the 54-year-old Palestinian mother returned from the departure station to her displacement tent on 5 November, an Israeli sniper shot and killed her.

“We are in shock,” Mohammed Sheikh al-Eid, Noura’s brother, told Middle East Eye.

“I lost my 14-year-old son during the famine, while he was trying to get aid. I swear to God, I did not grieve for him the way I have grieved for my sister,” he said.

“I considered her my second mother because she was the one who raised me.”

Since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, Israeli forces have repeatedly opened fire on Palestinians near the so-called "yellow line", which marks the boundary of areas under Israeli military control in Gaza.

Residents face indiscriminate gunfire from Israeli soldiers, military vehicles, lifters and quadcopters, including in areas beyond the line where civilians attempt to go about their daily lives.

‘Come back a doctor’

The night before Noura was killed, relatives gathered at their tent in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, to bid farewell to her husband, Atallah Abu Athra, and their daughter, Hiba Abu Athra.

“Her husband suffers from heart disease and diabetes, and his condition has deteriorated to the point where he developed gangrene,” Sheikh al-Eid said.

“Five of his toes and part of his foot had been amputated.” 

Israeli forces abuse Palestinians returning to Gaza at Rafah checkpoint
Read More »

Hiba had recently completed her secondary school exams. The family registered her as her father's medical companion so she could accompany him to Egypt and pursue her mother's dream of seeing her study medicine abroad.

At around 4am on the day of their departure, the family woke to prepare for the journey from their displacement tent to a Palestine Red Crescent centre, where buses carrying travellers to Egypt were departing.

“I told my Noura, ‘Just say goodbye to them here at the tent. You don't have to go with them.’ But she refused,” Sheikh al-Eid, 46, recalled.

“She accompanied them to the Red Crescent, along with her four other daughters. They said goodbye to her husband and daughter and waited until the bus had departed.”

Noura kissed Hiba and told her, in what would be her final words: “Come back to us as a doctor.”

She and her other daughters then went their separate ways. Only Rula accompanied Noura on the journey back to their tent.

The last ride home

Unable to find a car to take them home, Noura and Rula came across a man with a donkey-drawn cart who offered them a free ride.

“The road was extremely rough, and the donkey could not pull too much weight. The man told me that he could only take my mother because she seemed unwell. She had diabetes and felt dizzy,” Rula told MEE.

“I agreed and told him that what mattered was that my mother got a ride. She climbed onto the cart, and I walked right beside her,” the 18-year-old added. 

Right after Noura climbed aboard, some of her teeth fell to the ground, followed by a gush of blood from her mouth. She then collapsed. 

Gaza: Indiscriminate Israeli gunfire kills and terrorises displaced families
Read More »

Rula then heard what sounded like a small explosion.

“At first, I thought it was the sound of a ball or something, but then my mother’s teeth fell to the ground, blood began pouring from her mouth, and she fell off the cart,” Rula recounted.

“I still hadn’t realised that she had been shot. I thought she had fallen into a diabetic coma.”

People rushed to Noura's aid and took her to the British field hospital in al-Mawasi, western Khan Younis.

On the way to the hospital, Rula said her mother was still alive. She recited the Shahada [Islamic declaration of faith] and tried to say something, but Rula could not make out her words.

Eyewitnesses said Israeli forces routinely opened fire in the area. But nobody realised Noura had been hit by a bullet until she reached the hospital. 

At the hospital, a doctor examined Noura and showed those accompanying her where the bullet had entered beneath her lower jaw, near her teeth, and exited behind her right ear.

MEE viewed a post-mortem photograph of Noura’s face showing a narrow wound beneath her lower lip, apparently caused by the bullet that exited through the right side of her head.

“She was taken to the resuscitation room. But shortly after she arrived, a doctor came out and told me, ‘Your mother’s heart has stopped. She has passed away,’” Rula told MEE.

“I rushed to the resuscitation room and looked for her on the bed, but it was empty. I looked around and found her already wrapped in a shroud, lying beside the bed. I screamed and shouted at them, begging them to unwrap her so she could breathe.”

Israeli forces have killed at least 1,600 Palestinians since the October 2025 ceasefire, bringing the death toll since the beginning of the genocide to more than 74,000.

At least 196 were killed near the “yellow line” between 10 October 2025 and early April 2026, according to the United Nations’ Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel. 

They include 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls.

‘Hardest moment’

Doctors prepared Noura’s body for transfer to Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, where the family would make burial arrangements.

In the ambulance transporting her mother’s body, Rula sat silently beside her.

On the way, she spotted her maternal uncle, Mahmoud, running towards the British field hospital after receiving a call saying his sister was there. She asked the driver to stop and pick him up.

“He thought she had fallen into a diabetic coma. When he got into the ambulance, he asked me, ‘Where is your mother?’ I looked at the body and said, ‘Here she is. Don’t you see her? She is in the shroud,’” Rula said.

The family completed the burial arrangements and laid Noura, originally from Rafah, to rest in Khan Younis, where she had been displaced for more than two years.

'She was devastated, screaming and crying. We tried to comfort her, but she was in an unbearable state. She has not shed a single tear...  She is still in shock'

- Mohammed Sheikh al-Eid, Noura's brother 

But her husband and daughter, who were in Egypt, did not learn what had happened until the following day.

“We couldn’t tell them anything, but the next day, someone sent my sister a message offering condolences. She didn’t know who had died, so she searched online to find out who in our family had been killed,” Rula recalled.

“The [local] media had already reported what happened, and that was how she found out it was our mother.”

Sheikh al-Eid said none of Noura’s siblings could bring themselves to answer Hiba’s repeated calls after she learnt of her mother’s death.

“This was the hardest moment we went through… because we knew Hiba would blame herself, and we simply did not know what to say,” he said.

“We contacted relatives of her father in Egypt and asked them to go [and comfort] her. Once they arrived, they called us on a video call. She was devastated, screaming and crying. We tried to comfort her, but she was in an unbearable state.”

Since Noura was buried, her daughter Rula has barely spoken, Sheikh al-Eid told MEE.

“She has not shed a single tear. Even when she said goodbye to her mother [before burial], she did not cry at all. She is still in shock to this day,” he said.

Three of Noura’s daughters remain alone in their tent: Rula, 18; Saba, 16; and Ruwaida, 14.

Their uncle sends his wife to stay with them most of the time.

“We spent that night at my sister’s tent because we wanted to say goodbye to her daughter and husband,” he said.

“But in reality, we were saying goodbye to her.”

Israel's genocide in Gaza

item.title: Erdogan: Climate change is one of the 'deepest existential crises' in humanity's history
item.description:
Erdogan: Climate change is one of the 'deepest existential crises' in humanity's history

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has told the Cop31 summit that climate change is "one of the deepest existential crises" in humanity's history.

"I want to say this very clearly: we have no other sky, no other Earth, no other seas, oceans or forests," Erdogan said in a speech on Wednesday at the opening of the leaders' summit at the UN conference, which is being held in Turkey.

"Yet today, driven in part by the greed of excessive consumption, humanity is experiencing perhaps one of the deepest existential crises in its history," Turkey's president said.
